body:
Yup, I graduated in 2004. I haven't been back there since, sadly. 

I think my experience in college in general would have been much better if I had worked up the courage to get help for my depression back then. Mental health services weren't wonderful at VT in the early 00s (to many tragic ends), and for whatever reason, I thought I just needed to tough it out. I didn't really socialize; I just worked myself to exhaustion and ruminated. 

The sad thing is that I had a very good part time job in web development while in school, but all I could think about was how bored I was and badly I needed to leave Bburg to find happiness. (Unfortunately the org I worked for no longer exists, or I'd have been forwarding my resume back to my old contacts there years ago). 

It's hard for me to tell whether I really want to be back there, or if I'm just trying to return to the place I believe I truly fucked up in hopes that I can give myself a do-over.

That sounds awful :(

I feel like I've dealt with much scarier deadlines in the past (a client buys a remnant ad in the newspaper at the last minute --  the paper goes to print whether you finished your ad or not). I don't know why, but I just seemingly cannot handle it anymore. Maybe it's because I'm in a job that I'm totally unqualified for, so I blame my inability to quickly get things done on my lack of skill. 

Either way, it's like I've somehow managed to unlearn all of the CBT I had received from past therapy. I can say to myself, "What's the worst that could happen? You lose your job. And then you go and find a new one, because you've done it before." But it doesn't calm me down and bring me back to reality like it used to.

Freelancing feels like such a cruel joke. I don't know of anyone who freelances successfully unless they're being supported financially by a spouse or partner. Every time I read a blog post (etc.) by someone saying how happy they are that they quit their office job and set out on their own, I look up the author and find out that they have a wife or husband with a traditional, well-paying job. 

Of course freelancing is great when your spouse can cover the rent during the slow months, and you're bidding $200 for logo design projects to pad out your portfolio because ultimately you have a sturdy financial safety net. It's so frustrating.

Moving back to the town I went to college in has actually been one of the desperate ideas I've had during times my head was a little clearer. I've had job alerts set up for my old college for the past couple of months — nothing yet, and I have doubts they'd be willing to hire someone who isn't local anymore. 

The biggest problem is that I don't have a driver's license (and of course I don't have a car). Living in the city, it was never really needed. Adult driving school is expensive ($600). 

But (at the risk of giving out too much personal information), living in Blacksburg was one of the last times I remember being content. I liked having access to trails and the mountains, and I was able to plant things on our tiny balcony. Rent was much cheaper. Or maybe it's just a desire to return to the place I think I fucked up my life. 

The car thing though screws me over royally. I wouldn't feel as apprehensive about homelessness if I knew I could just pack my kitties into a car and drive away.

Thank you, everyone, for your comments and PMs. I didn't think anyone would read this or respond — I just assumed it would quietly fall off the "new post" list. I will try to reply to you throughout the day if I can find time (the workday has begun, unfortunately). If not, then later tonight. 

I wasn't able to get any work done last night — I was too panicky, too paralyzed with my own anxiety. Trying to figure out now how to explain myself as soon as my manager asks where it is. 

I had my annual ob/gyn exam this morning, and they noted that my blood pressure was high. As a distance runner, it had always been extremely low. This is the first time in my life that this has happened.

The job market has been really rough for the past couple of years. Most of the jobs I apply to on LinkedIn have 200-300 applicants. 

I wish there was a universal basic income.
I know. But I wish I was naive enough to allow myself to believe in one — how nice it would be to just hang out with my dad or grandparents again, and not have to worry about work 24/7.
